title: Isochrone Map: Travel-Time Polygons
description: Draw travel-time polygons along the road network with the Isochrone Map — drive, cycle or walk reach, as shapes instead of circles. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 30-minute drive-time polygon around a city depot covers the motorway corridor generously and the river's far bank barely — the shape roads actually allow.
quick_answer: The Isochrone Map draws the area reachable within a set travel time from one origin, following the road network for driving, cycling or walking. Set the place, mode and minutes and read the polygon — the honest shape of reach that a radius circle only pretends to be.

Response-time duties are isochrone duties: the polygon is the area a station can honestly claim. Population inside it is the next number, from the population tools.
Draw the 45-minute polygon from the office and house-hunt inside the shape, not inside a circle that includes the estuary.
One isochrone teaches more transport geography than a chapter of text: networks, barriers and corridors are all visible at once.

A 30-minute driving polygon stretches far along fast roads and barely across slow ones. Two homes the same crow-miles from work can sit one inside and one outside the shape — that is the entire argument for drawing it.
The 20-minute walking polygon is a compact blob around the origin; the 20-minute driving one is a starburst along the arterials. Same minutes, different cities — mode is a geography of its own.

popular_table.title: Isochrone or radius — which shape?
popular_table.intro: Two ways to draw reach. This page is the network column; the Map Radius Tool owns the circle column.
popular_table.note: Isochrones are only as current as the network data beneath them; a new bridge redraws the shape the day the data learns about it.

faq: Is this the same as the Drive Time Map?

Cousins, not twins: both draw travel-time reach from the road network. This page is organised around the isochrone concept and its modes; the Drive Time Map around the depot-and-minutes planning workflow. The polygons agree because the network is shared.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Times are the network's typical speeds, not this minute's congestion. Peak-hour reality is slower; the shape is the free-flow truth.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Roads wind — and isochrones exist precisely because reach follows roads, not geometry.
Can route results change over time?
Yes: new roads and reclassified streets reshape polygons as the open data updates. Re-draw before a decision, not from memory.
Driving, cycling and walking, each on its legal network — the walk polygon uses paths a car cannot, and vice versa.
How many time bands can I draw?
Several rings at once — nested isochrones (10/20/30 minutes) are the classic catchment picture this tool is built for.
The reach shapes are the working output of the page; the site's export tools elsewhere handle GPX and data formats for routes.
Why is my polygon not a neat set of rings?
Because roads are not neat. Lobes along fast corridors and bites where barriers sit are the information — a neat shape would be the lie.
This tool draws typical-speed shapes, closer to the free-flow case. Rush-hour polygons shrink; schedule the real trip with margin the map cannot give you.
